name: Marco Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the flow-wrappers after the ovens at Hartley’s Biscuits, setting film, centring the print and checking the seals. I have done it sixteen years with a vocational certificate, and the wage is about average for this job. When a seal runs cold, packets open in the shop and I hear about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Gina works at a dental front desk; our school-age son Leo and daughter live with us, and we have a mortgage. We have about three months saved and some other factories nearby. I use AI now and then for dull letters, once I have seen someone else get a useful result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the packing end that AI is useful for forms and not much else in this picture. A letter it helped me write got our energy bill corrected, so I am not against a useful tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flow-wrapper still needs me watching the film seam and print mark. Gina’s dental reception wage and my usual biscuit-plant pay cover the mortgage, and three months saved means a short stoppage would be manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my day shifts, check the packet seals and coach Leo’s football team at weekends. I would keep using AI now and then for household letters, as I already do, and put any fresh overtime wages left after bills into our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about the job. Chocolate biscuit day would still smell better than any software demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the seam goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cold seal opens in the shop, so I stop the line and check the heat setting. A missed print mark makes the wrapper look cheap even if the biscuit is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new kitchen now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gina and I want one, but only after the mortgage and three-month reserve stay covered. A calm AI story would not make the fitting cost disappear.

say: I would say **useful forms** are fine without expecting a factory revolution.
I would still watch the **packet seam** and print mark.
think: Two **usual wages** and three months saved can cover a short stoppage.
do: Keep **day shifts** and check seals and print marks.
Keep using **household AI letters** as I already do.
Save fresh **overtime wages** only after bills are covered.
feel: **Calm** about familiar work and a manageable reserve.
S0.quote: The flow-wrapper still needs me watching the film seam and print mark.
fieldNote: Marco’s occasional **AI letter use** is an existing habit rather than a new skill.
He builds savings only from **new paid overtime**, while the kitchen remains a conditional household purchase.

steps.text: Keep flow-wrapper day shifts and check packet seals
Save fresh overtime wages left after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm has to keep up with customers, but operators deserve a fair chance at the better machine jobs. I have seen two colleagues move into maintenance after a paid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Software could take planning and ordering quickly; a camera wrapper may later do my print alignment. If the packing crew loses shifts, Gina’s receptionist pay alone will not carry the mortgage and the children’s costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for Hartley’s next funded six-month maintenance course if it includes paid shift time and a safe stopped-wrapper place. If accepted, I would enrol and practise on the machine; I would also learn a new AI error-code guide on our wrapper only after an offered paid demonstration and check its advice against the manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the packing hours, but there is a route worth testing. A place on the course matters more than another poster in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who showed you the course worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dean and Sal both finished last year and got better-paid maintenance posts. I would still ask whether a place is open this year and whether the wage and hours suit our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid course place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my wrapper shift and check posted nearby operator jobs at a wage we can live on. I would not take unpaid evenings away from the children for a course with no actual place.

say: I would ask for **operator access** to real maintenance places.
I would keep the firm **competitive** while protecting paid instruction.
think: A **camera wrapper** could remove my alignment hours.
Gina’s **reception wage** cannot carry our mortgage alone after a cut.
do: Apply for **funded maintenance training** with paid safe practice; enrol only if accepted.
Learn the **new AI error guide** after paid instruction and verify against the manual.
Check **posted local operator jobs** at adequate pay if no place opens.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, with a proven route to test.
S1.quote: A place on the course matters more than another poster in the canteen.
fieldNote: His **steady adaptability** follows colleagues’ successful paid training rather than untested promises.
The **AI guide** is new learning, conditional on offered paid instruction, and the job fallback has no hours-cut trigger.

steps.text: Enrol only if accepted for funded paid maintenance course with safe stopped-wrapper practice place
Learn new AI error guide after offered paid instruction and manual checks
Check posted nearby adequate-pay operator jobs if no course place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the packing team thinking AGI might arrive in 2028 while capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. The office could change first, but robots changing film reels would hit our shifts later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the wrapper crew to lose most paid hours if the robots can load film and clean safely. The three-month reserve is real, but it cannot carry Gina, Leo, our daughter and the mortgage through a long wage loss; I wake at night over that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the plant for written staffing dates, cancel the planned kitchen and new car, and save a fresh part of each full wage month while work lasts. If my paid hours end, I would take offered paid Saturday tiling with my brother-in-law Rob only when he has a real customer booking, and apply for posted reachable factory or trades jobs paying enough for our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by a likely large wage loss. Saturday tiles might buy groceries, but they cannot replace the biscuit-plant wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Rob have enough tiling work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He has occasional extra jobs, not a full second wage for me. I would ask him for confirmed paid dates and bring my own safety gear before counting a penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no adequate job is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lender about a temporary mortgage plan before missing a payment. I would keep any paid wrapper shifts still offered rather than call a search a job.

say: I would distinguish **2028 office AGI** from 2031 film-changing robots.
I would ask for **real staffing dates** on the packing line.
think: I expect **most wrapper hours** to vanish after capable robots arrive.
Three **months saved** cannot bridge a long loss of my wage.
do: Request **staffing dates**, cancel kitchen and car plans, and save new wages while shifts last.
Take **paid tiling dates** only if Rob has confirmed customer work after hours end.
Apply after **lost hours** for posted reachable bill-covering factory or trades work.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and broken sleep.
S2.quote: I would be alarmed by a likely large wage loss.
fieldNote: He expects a **major factory-income loss** after hands-on robots, with thinking work changing first.
Tiling is **confirmed paid side work**, while an adequate posted job and possible lender agreement remain uncertain.

steps.text: Cancel kitchen and car plans and save fresh paid wages
Take paid tiling dates after lost hours only with confirmed customers
Apply after lost hours for posted reachable bill-covering jobs
Ask lender for temporary plan if no adequate job appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the football parents that thinking AGI in 2031 comes before robots that can change film around 2034. Five years is enough to test a different paid skill without leaving a secure shift tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I will still need the mortgage wage. Maintenance might last longer than watching packets, but a certificate helps only if Hartley’s or another nearby plant actually posts paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for the funded paid-time engineering course if Hartley’s offers a stopped-machine place, and enrol if accepted. After qualifying I would apply for a posted reachable maintenance role at bill-covering pay; separately I would take paid Saturday tiling with Rob when customers book, transferring actual new tiling earnings toward tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious but able to work through the dates. A course, a vacancy and a customer booking are three separate things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise on the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would isolate a stopped wrapper, replace a worn seal jaw and restart under a qualified fitter. I would not learn by reaching into a live machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Hartley’s has no maintenance vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check posted openings at the other reachable plants and keep my paid wrapper shifts. The certificate would not let us move for a lower wage.

say: I would ask for **paid engineering places** before 2034 robots.
I would separate **2031 thinking work** from later physical change.
think: The **mortgage wage** will still matter every month when I am forty-eight.
A **maintenance certificate** needs a posted adequate role to be useful.
do: Apply for **funded paid-time engineering** with safe stopped-machine practice; enrol only if accepted.
Apply after **qualification** for a posted reachable bill-covering maintenance job.
Take **confirmed paid tiling** with Rob and save new earnings for tools.
feel: **Anxious**, with time for a staged plan.
S3.quote: A course, a vacancy and a customer booking are three separate things.
fieldNote: Marco tests **maintenance and tiling** as separate paid paths instead of assuming either succeeds.
Training requires **funded paid safe practice**, while applications and tiling require adequate postings or booked customers.

steps.text: Enrol only if accepted for funded paid engineering course with safe stopped-machine practice
Apply after qualification for posted reachable bill-covering maintenance role
Take paid Saturday tiling only with confirmed customer booking
Save actual new tiling earnings toward tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI around 2036 and capable hands-on robots around 2039 give us time to make a proper choice. Families and firms should both plan from paid work, not a sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three in 2036 and fifty-six when wrapper robots may arrive. The children may be grown, but I cannot assume the mortgage is gone or that tiling demand stays strong every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the biscuit-plant shifts and take paid tiling dates with Rob when booked. If four years of paid tiling prove steady and six months of expenses are saved from new wages, I would buy a van and tools we can afford, then leave Hartley’s for the bathroom business only after confirmed customers cover our bills; in the first year after 2036 I would keep that business only while it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy rather than crushed. The long clock gives me room to test customers before we rely on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on six months first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: January can be quiet for bathrooms, while Hartley’s pays the same each month. I would not give up that wage with only a few good Saturdays behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if robot tilers become good too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would reassess actual booked work and posted local jobs before buying more equipment. I would keep a cash buffer instead of promising that home repairs are immune.

say: I would plan from **paid tiling bookings**, not sales claims.
I would separate **2036 AGI** from 2039 physical robots.
think: The **mortgage and January demand** remain uncertain thirteen years out.
I can test **bathroom customers** while factory wages still arrive.
do: Keep **current plant shifts** and take paid booked tiling dates.
Buy **van and tools** only after steady paid demand and six months newly saved.
Leave for **bathroom work** only when confirmed customer income covers household bills.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to test demand and build a cushion.
S4.quote: I would keep a cash buffer instead of promising that home repairs are immune.
fieldNote: His **2026 factory work** is current; a business after 2036 requires paid customers and household-covering income.
The **van purchase and exit** require four years of proven bookings and six months saved from actual new pay.

steps.text: Keep plant shifts and take booked paid tiling dates
Buy affordable van and tools after four steady years and six months saved
Leave Hartley’s only when confirmed bathroom income covers household bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it leaves little time to prove that maintenance or tiling can carry our bills before capable robots reach the wrappers. A funded paid safe course, written staffing dates and posted reachable jobs at adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the biscuit smell. I will miss chocolate day if I ever leave the plant, even if I find better pay somewhere else.

headlineQuote: I will miss chocolate day if I ever leave the plant, even if I find better pay somewhere else.
portrait: **Marco**, 43, runs biscuit flow-wrappers and checks film alignment and seals after sixteen years with a vocational certificate.
His **dental-reception partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, ordinary pay and three-month reserve give some room to test a path.
He uses **AI occasionally** for household letters and would learn a new error guide only with proven paid instruction.
He weighs **funded maintenance training** against confirmed paid tiling, with a bathroom business conditional on customers and savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to test enough replacement pay before physical robots threaten wrapper shifts.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded paid safe course**, written staffing dates and posted reachable bill-covering work would help.
